utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, or whatever time it may be for you, for anyone in and around this courtroom and the videolink room. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We hear the testimony of the next witness to be called by the Defence through videolink. Let's first establish whether the videolink is functioning well. Could the representative of the Registry at the other side of the videolink first confirm whether he can hear us and whether he can see us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. We can hear you and see you well. I hope you can do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you and see you as well. Thank you for this information. We see that you are present in the videolink room together with a person which I assume will be the witness. Is there anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] There is no one else present in the videolink room. This is only me and Mr. Del Pino.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I take it that you have a fixed camera and a fixed audio-recording system.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct. And we have a technician right next door in case there is a glitch but, for now, we're all alone in this room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I take it that with you is the witness, Mr. Del Pino.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Del Pino, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. Could I invite you to stand and to make the solemn declaration of which the text is handed out to you by the representative of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Del Pino. Please be seated. Mr. Del Pino, you'll be first examined by the -- by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic, and you'll see him soon our your screen. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Del Pino. I'm glad to finally meet you, albeit over the TV screen. Could I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: My name is David Del Pino Kloques.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, one preliminary matter. The original Rule 65 ter summary for this witness incorrectly noted that he was part of the oversight committee when in fact he was interviewed by the oversight committee. We did address -- fix that in the second filing, but I'm told that the original filing is still on record and so I did want to point that out so that everyone is on the same page as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to please tell us what is your current occupation and employment.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I'm a educational technologist. I'm the Assistant Director for Business and Economic Systems at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I already invite you to slow down because with your speed of speech the interpreters will not be able to translate -- to interpret your words so that we can consider them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. I will repeat my answer then. I'm an educational technologist. I work for the University of Texas Medical Branch. My title is Assistant Director for Business and Economic Systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, what educational degrees do you hold?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I'm an anthropologist. I do have computer certification in a few different areas, and I have a masters degree in educational technologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And prior to today, have you ever had occasion to testify as a witness in any court proceeding?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And were you ever in Bosnia-Herzegovina for purposes of any of your previous employments?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: No, I never was a witness before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. Were you ever present in Bosnia-Herzegovina for purposes of any of your previous employments?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Bosnia working for Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your specific position or title at the time that you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I was a forensic expert. I done field-work, assisting the archaeological phases of the work, and I was involved in the laboratory work, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what had been your specific job or occupation prior to going to Bosnia as part of Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I was a forensic anthropologist since 1989, working in human rights violations, missing persons cases in my country, in Chile. And I'm the founding member of our forensic team, which was the DAF Chilean forensic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And apart from the Chilean anthropological forensic team, were you ever a member of any other professional associations dealing with anthropology?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Not really. I worked with Dr. Glasno [phoen] and he is my master, my mentor in forensics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall what year it was that you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina performing the work that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how long in 1996 you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I think it was from June to November, late June to early November, something like that. I'm not exactly clear about the exact dates. But from summer to the beginning of winter or the ending of fall season.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Do you recall the names of any other anthropologist whom you may have worked with while in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes. Jose Baraybar, I think is the last name. I perhaps not recall the names but I recall the people. Gallagher, a student, Kliakov [phoen] another young anthropologist at the time, and Moscosko, an archaeologist. There was a wealth of people that I remember in personal ways but not clearly the names. There was an anthropologist from the USA -- archaeologist from the USA. I'm trying to recall his name but I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me see if I can assist you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I know the people. I can recognise the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know anyone by the name of C. Elliot Moore also known by the nickname Hass?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes. He was working for -- I think he was related to the army here in the USA, looking for missing soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was his profession, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall anyone by the name of Clyde Snow?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Dr. Clyde Snow is my mentor. He passed away but I do remember very well. He's part of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand. Now, do you recall which specific sites --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're done with the names. You mentioned the name of Gallagher. You said it was a student. Was it a male or a female, and do you remember any first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dorothy Gallagher. Yes, sir. Dorothy Gallagher was a lady, a female.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's Dorothy Gallagher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall any of the specific sites that you were asked to work on as part of the mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I do recall all the sites. I don't recall the name of the sites. And names and pictures in my mind are a little mixed up, so I would need some of your help to identify. But I do remember exactly the work in every single site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you worked on a number of sites, not just one?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough for our purposes. What, if anything, were you told about who or what was at the sites that were being excavated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean by "who or what"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were what were you told to expect at the sites that were being excavated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. One second. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, but could we get who he is being told anything by so we can get that right up front and perhaps when.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's my second question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think there was any reason to intervene. Would you please continue your answer. You started by saying -- no, not anything yet. Could you tell us what you were told to expect at the sites that were being excavated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was told to expect mass graves. And I was before working for the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia with a similar team, so I was told to expect a similar excavation situation with a mass grave, semi-decomposed bodies, and so forth. So I had the mindset for what I was going to encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if could I ask you to address the question raised by Mr. McCloskey. Do you recall by whom you were told to expect this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: We got some documentation in print form by Physicians for Human Rights, and I briefly talked to Haglund, Bill Haglund, and that's how I got information to be prepared for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said that you had previously worked with a similar team working for the International Tribunal. Were you ever directed by anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal during either of your engagements?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: What do you mean by "directed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Given directions.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: No. I was a member of the forensic team. The Tribunal -- I wasn't aware of the presence of the Tribunal at the sites, but perhaps they were there. And we had guards. I think they made us feel secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Whom did you consider to be in charge of the operation from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Haglund, Bill Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what exactly was your job; that is to say, how did you understand your role within the operation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: At the time I was a little older than the rest of the crew, and so I had a -- Haglund would put me in different jobs as needed because I was able to perform most of the duties required in excavation, and so I had done a wealth of different tasks as needed per site. For example, photographer, for example, direct excavation, for example, taking measurements. And then I work at the laboratory in my capacity as an anthropologist, and that's -- I cleaned bones, I reassembled broken bones, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did anyone talk about determining if a set of remains belonged to a combatant or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: We were -- I think that question wasn't part of the forensic research we were doing. We were in a discovery mode, in my mind at least; we were going to find out. Having that question before was not proper. For example, digging in Europe, you can find grave-sites from any war you guys involved yourselves like, say, 40 years. So it was a discovery process, a scientific approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, generally speaking, when someone is engaging in scientific approach excavating a potential grave-site, are there normally protocols that are established; and if, so, what we would be?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes. Forensic archaeology is extremely conscientious about keeping the relationships in between the elements you are going to take -- lifting from the grave. We're supposed to know that every time you intervene in a grave you are rescuing information and destroying information at the same time. So that's why it's so important, the graphical record of elements you are getting from the grave, how they are related to each other. For example, if you found a body and its clothing, is the body inside the clothing or not? Or if you find a key chain next to a body, how far it was, where it goes, and so forth. Or in a mass grave, the position of the bodies, how they are co-mingled together. So all those relationships are extremely important at the time of bringing about a reconstruction of how these bodies were put together in that archaeological site. So relationships for us is really important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation --

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Did I answer what you were asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think so. I have a follow-up. In relation to what you have talked about in relation to forensic archaeology and anthropology, when doing excavation of graves, what is the normal procedure for clothing and artefacts found with the human remains?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: You try to keep them together. If they are not -- because of the construction of the grave, usually they -- the grave-site is constructed in a way that in the case of human rights violation, it's constructed in a very quick way. Usually criminals are trying to hide what they've done. And so sometimes the bodies are very well preserved and all together with the clothing and documents and so forth. But sometimes you get a grave-site in which clothing or the cultural elements are separated from the dead bodies, implying a sort of activity before the burial. And that's important, too. To me as an archaeologist, I need to see and I need to evaluate even if the elements are separated. It's evidence to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say that it's important to you. What kinds of information as an anthropologist or archaeologist can be established from clothing and other artefacts found with human remains?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Without even looking at the clothing and artefacts, you can -- you get information by knowing how they were around the body, how the grave-site was constructed. Now, if you -- if you establish a proper relationship in between the clothing and the bodies that own the clothing or are related to the clothing, then you can dig a little deeper. If there are cultural objects together with the clothing, like photo IDs, keys, and so forth, then you can think about establishing a relationship in those extra elements that will come with your -- as an evidence and the relationship to the original individual you are digging out will give you a good clue of what's the relationship between the rest of the evidence and the body. So, yeah. Do you have any follow-up?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Apart from the excavations that you took part in in Bosnia-Herzegovina which you've just described, do you have an estimate as to how many total excavations you have been involved in throughout your career?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Oh, my Lord. A lot. In my country, I've done several forensic digs and in different situations, but I -- the number is -- is -- I think it's below 500. Below 500 individuals. But above 250 -- no, no, above 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: That's a rough number. I'm sorry, but I never counted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you say about 500 individuals. The question was how many excavation sites, if I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll say about 15 or 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. Now, in anthropological field recovery, first of all, is that term that are you familiar with, "field recovery"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: It's what you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In field recovery, what is considered to be associated evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I mean, this is a -- it depends on your research. But from the beginning, the whole grave-site is a -- it gives you evidence. When you just -- even before getting anything from the ground, you are recovering the activities of producing the burial. So the wealth of information is started when you get to the site. Is that a good answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the answer that you've given. That's all I am requiring from you, sir, is the answers as you know them. I'm not here to qualify or judge them. And in relation to the examination of associated evidence in field recovery, is there a procedure for preserving such associated evidence that is commonly followed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You normally produce a -- you're supposed to have paperwork in which you are writing down the evidence. You're going around the body. You're supposed to draw a rough draw of the circumstances of the body and the elements surrounding it. Then you're supposed to picture it. You will see a wealth of photography being taken around any forensic dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: And sometimes people choose to do videos of the whole burial at the time of recovering the evidence so no relationships are going to be lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the work that you took part in in Bosnia-Herzegovina which we have been talking about, who was in charge of removing and documenting the bodies, the artefacts, and the associated evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: The sites were so big that we split in teams, and small teams in different segments of graves. And one person was taking notes and two other people were cleaning up the body and taking -- getting the photographs to get a graphical -- the graphical evidence. That's what's -- normally we shoot to do. We target to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any guidelines or protocols were established and followed for the excavation of those sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes. We had a form to fill and we tried to -- we set some parametres of the work. For example, we were -- I think that's the answer. We have our little small team: Somebody taking notes, somebody covering the photographer, somebody cleaning the body, two people getting the body out. That's the method.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your opinion -- what is your opinion of the level of communication in the field between the various other specialties that were working alongside anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: In the -- in the grave-sites, the communication was rather okay, but sometimes we did not have a -- Dr. Haglund would be absent sometimes, and that will make the work more difficult because we -- basically there was not a chain of command properly organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in the field of anthropology, what is the process known as trauma analysis?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: You're bringing me now to the laboratory work. Yeah. For trauma analysis, you clean the body the best you can to look at the morphology of the bones, and then you can isolate, for example, all injuries early fractures and with a -- the bone will clearly reveal the life history of the trauma of the person. And there are certain markings on the bone that will clearly indicate sometimes injuries that are not healed or the body wasn't able to react to it, so we established perimortem or recent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have a question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Finish your answer. Please finish your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I thought somebody was saying something there. So perimortem, you can identify the type of trauma, sometimes blunt trauma, sometimes they are projectiles of different velocities and you can sort it out by looking at the types of entrance and exit wounds, if they are marking the bones, and cut marks, that that's very clearly isolated -- easy to isolate. So that's something that will go into an anthropological forensic report. Together with that we can do a lot of other things, for example, laterality, to see if the person used to use more the left or the right side of the body, and we can see statistically with certain/uncertainty the height and sometimes very clearly the sex of the person. On top that, it's easy at a certain age to estimate the biological age of the skeleton and so there's a lot of things you can do, really, depending on your skill level, how can you listen to the skeleton, the life history and how he died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Earlier you said, sir, that Dr. Haglund would be absent sometimes and the chain of command would not be in place. Was Dr. Haglund the leader of the team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was the leader of the team, but he split his time at several sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in his absence did he not have a deputy to deputise for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mean, not to my knowledge, and I was working for him. So a few people trying to take over the second on board but it was not -- to me, at least, it was not very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, for the process that you have described for trauma analysis in the lab, can clothing worn by a body have a role assisting in that examination?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This is no different to what I say about archaeology. That's why you recover the relationships between the elements at the grave. The clothing is one of your components of analysis. Yes, it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in your experience at the sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina where you were involved in doing the work, were all clothing and artefacts found during the excavation preserved and kept with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I would say in most of the case, yes. But I was in one of the grave-sites in which some of the clothing were discarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned a Mr. Baraybar. What was the role of Mr. Baraybar in the work that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't really know. He was joining with us as a team member, working for Haglund, but then I understood that he was working for UN as a forensic team of UN, and he had a different role and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding what his different role and responsibility were as opposed to the work that you were doing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Sometimes Jose Pablo Baraybar will join as a team member, as a peer of us, and we worked together okay and -- but I don't know any -- any other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on. At an excavation site, what is the importance, if any, of protecting human remains and artefacts from the elements, such as rain?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Oh, it's of extreme importance because any foreign intrusion, like rain, on the grave-site can remove the liaison in between the elements you are seeing in the grave, and you can lose -- even though can you recover everything, you lose the connections, and the connections is evidence you need to gather in order to produce information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In your experience, were the human remains and artefacts in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the sites that you have knowledge of, were they always adequately protected from the elements such as rain?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I say most of the time but not all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you completed your work in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you interviewed by anybody about the work that was performed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, but the San Antonio group of analysis, I mean, I was part of the San Antonio report, as you know. That was in 1997, after the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if you were told the purpose of why you were being interviewed by this San Antonio Analysis Group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes. They were trying to -- they were trying to research about the method we had done at the grave-sites and -- that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't remember the names, but I know Dr. DiMaio was there, which was one of the forensic authors I followed the most when I was studying forensics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during your interview did you identify any concerns to those that interviewed you about the manner in which the work was done at grave-sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Exactly what I shared with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now take a look at Exhibit D329 with you. There should be a hard copy there with Mr. Registrar. And this should be a report of the oversight committee.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Is this the San Antonio report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. That's what I was going to ask you. Sir, is this the report that you mentioned that you call the San Antonio report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Correct, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to page 2 of the report with you, and at the bottom it says: "Part 3, Interviewing Process. Following a briefing by an ICTY attorney on Saturday, November 15, 1997, interviews of the team members were conducted on an individual basis in the office, beginning on Sunday, November 16, 1997. During the first two days, the interviewees were: Connor, Curran, Gallagher, Hoffmann, Koff, Del Pino, Snow and Saunders." Does what is written here accord with your recollection of how the interview process took place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't recall the event so much but this is very sound to me. I think it is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now turn to page 5 of this document and if we could focus on item number 14 here, there appears to be some language next to your name that I'd like to ask you about. It says: "David Del Pino (Chilean Anthropologist): Operations were halted when Dr. Haglund was away. Clothing was discarded at Haglund's command, even though some contained identifications. Forms were not always used. There was no delegation of authority." Do you believe that this language accurately reflects the comments you made when you were interviewed in 1997 by the San Antonio committee?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: That's precise. It is indeed what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you tell the truth to the members of the committee that interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to clothing being discarded at Mr. Haglund's command, do you recall if any reason was given for this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: He believed that the clothing was not related with the bodies and to me that was a research question, not something that you can see at the site. You need to lift all the evidence. I think I told Dr. Haglund that at the time of the site. We have a disagreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else voice objection to the discarding of clothing at the site?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the quantity of such clothing that was discarded?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: This is 18 years ago, so it was -- it was not a huge amount of clothing, but it was a volume, say, of about 50 litres maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall if any of the clothing discarded was military or civilian in nature?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: The clothing, that will be a research question. You cannot say that on the site. You need to clean the clothing. And it will be imprecise if I answered that one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. I thank you for that answer. Do you know who actually discarded the clothing after Dr. Haglund commanded it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here you say "even though some contained identification." What happened to the identification?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: That part of the sentence is not precise. I should have -- it should have been written there "some may contain."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if they did --

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: It's part of the research.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: It's part of the research. It's a question. That's why I will never discard stuff from the grave-site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you say that you had a disagreement with Dr. Haglund. In your opinion, was the discarding of clothing potentially with identifications in accord with the generally accepted practices applicable to excavations, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: It's not am acceptable practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know if anyone made a determination if the clothing had any identification before it was discarded?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could turn to page 7 in the document, I'd like to focus your attention at the top of the page where we have some text which reads: "Several anthropologists believed and had alleged that the scientific integrity of the exhumations had been jeopardized because Dr. Haglund spent too much time playing up to the news media and driving around the country-side. Several believed he had capriciously and arbitrarily speeded up or slowed down the exhumations to accommodate the news media or to frustrate photographers." Sir, do you recall if you were one of the anthropologists who made such comments to the San Antonio Group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: That was a perception of not only me but the rest of -- some other members of the crew. But I need to say that -- that you can reduce the precision level of the information you get from the site but not to zero. I mean, there are some very valuable information getting from these grave-sites, even in these conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood. Now, if we could turn to page 9 of this document, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the next page, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom we see at item number 9, "Discussion and Conclusion," and on the next page, we have a list going from 1 to 14 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That will be page 10, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be page 10. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it says, "There is mutual agreement on management problems on the part of supervisors." And I'd like to ask you about a few of these. If we could focus on number 7, which says --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me read it and see if we're on the same page. Number 7 should read: "There was little need for rapidity of some grave-site exhumations" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now had a -- yes, could you please restart because a different page was shown to us a minute ago when you started reading, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Number 7: "There was little need for rapidity of some grave-site exhumations and only one exhumation should have been performed at one time." Do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Not really. This statement is a little unfair and imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: If you rephrase it in the following manner, that only one grave-site should be open at any given time, considering the size of the team, I would say that. But he had more than one grave-site running at the same time. But the rapidity of each exhumation in a mass grave is really, really a factor of how the bodies are co-mingled. So, for example, in a mass grave, where the construction of the site involved machinery, you can see that the bodies are all twisted around, so you will have to exhumate more than one body at the same time, making the archaeological phases a little more difficult but not impossible. I mean, if you rephrase this conclusion that way, I will totally agree that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, if we could look at number 10 together, which reads: "There was no attempt to schedule or co-ordinate anthropological and pathological investigations." Do you have any comments as to this statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I was not high enough in the chain of command to see whether -- how the organisation was going on. It was being implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: So I cannot confirm. But, yeah, it's difficult for me to estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And the last part of this list I want to look at is number 11, which reads: "There was too much concern with regard to media involvement." Do you agree with this --

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, that was a -- yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can turn to the next page in the document, which is entitled, "Section 7, Committee Recommendations," I think I would like to ask you about number 4 at the top of the page, which reads as follows: "Develop a standard operating procedure for the collection and handling of evidence (pathological, anthropological, and criminal)." Do you agree with this recommendation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with this recommendation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the operating procedure standardized in Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the work that others were doing alongside yourself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: In the sites I was involved with, we were consistent in following the same pattern of collection -- collecting information. I'm not a -- we didn't know what the other sites were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And one last area for you, sir. In our trial, at transcript page 14496 through 14498, the Prosecution presented a textile expert, Ms. Susan Meyers, who said that "videotaping fabric and then not preserving the fabric makes it impossible to run further tests on the fabric because you need the material itself." Do you agree with the comments of Ms. Meyers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Partially. I'm not an expert in fabric, of course, but I do forensic research -- I used to do forensic research. And even though the fabric is required, you are still having a lot of information from a decent image collection. For example, you can estimate the make of the fabric, you can research the colour of the fabric, you can count the thread of the fabric, and so forth, even though you may not have the actual fabric. But that is not my domain of expertise. I'm just -- if I'm producing a document about a mass grave or so and I don't have the fabric, I will go with the pictures. I would be able to describe some meaningful items for the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then, sir, my last question in relation to the clothing items that were discarded upon the command of Dr. Haglund, were those photographed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. We're close to the time where we take a break. Perhaps it would be better not to start with the cross-examination for a couple of minutes. But I would have one follow-up question, Mr. Del Pino. Just for my understanding, when you said that the volume or the quantity, I think the question was about the quantity of the discarded clothing was 50 litres, just to make sure that we understand each other well, that would be approximately a box of 40 centimetres by 40 centimetres and then a little bit over 30 centimetres high? Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's a proper understanding of what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you tell us, the clothing of how many persons, if you can establish that or assess that, the number -- the clothing of how many persons would fit into a box of such size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really because you see the mud in Europe, especially in Bosnia, is a type of -- obviously, mud will stick with the clothing unless you wash it so -- enlarge the volume of each piece. So I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you also have no clue as to the clothing of how many persons would have been discarded --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The volume I remember in my mind, but it's a volume of dirty clothing, with mud and materials. So it would be impossible for me to recall -- to make you an approximation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even in terms of whether it would be five or 30 or 80 or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the clothing were co-mingled and packed together and the mud and the accumulation of material was around the clothing, in this 50 litres, it would clothing for, like, a lot of people. But if mud is intrusive and occupying layers in between the pack of clothing, it would be very few people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Don't force yourself to draw any conclusions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you think you couldn't draw. Thank you for having answered this question. We'll take a break, and we'd like to continue in 20 minutes from now. For our local time, that would be 20 minutes past 3.00. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first establish whether the videolink is still functioning well? Can you hear me at the videolink room and see us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, we can still see and hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we can hear and see you also. Mr. Del Pino, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. And as he will do, you're also invited to make a short break between question and answer and answer and question. Mr. McCloskey, we have high expectations in that respect of your performance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And hello, Mr. Del Pino.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't take too much of your time today. Don't hold that against us. This Court has heard weeks of evidence about forensic anthropology and archaeology and the work. I would like to see if I can help refresh your recollection about one particular grave and ask you some questions about it. I believe at the time it was called the Pilica grave. It should have been probably the biggest grave you worked on. And let me show you a couple of pictures, just to help to see if that refreshes your recollection. If we could start with 65 ter 335826 and it will be page 8 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Check the number. I think there's too many digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, 65 ter 33526, page 8, which is -- it's one exhibit in the 65 ter with several pages to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're not looking at you anymore but hopefully we're looking at this big picture. Does that bring back any memories?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 7, same 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Eleven, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does this look like the same grave to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Can you go back and forth, please. I don't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness invites us to go back one page as well on our screens so that we know what he's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a different view of the same grave, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just stay on this number 7 for a minute, and I know it may be hard, but do you recognise anybody in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes. The person looking down with the hat is Jose Pablo Baraybar. The person standing with the shirt with lines is, if you -- the name doesn't come to me but I recognise him as an American forensic archaeologist working for the military in the recovery of missing soldiers. And the other people is French security guards. And the blond person in the picture I think is an UN deminer, a member of the team, the deminer team, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go to another picture --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, this is the -- this is another picture of the Pilica grave. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe to us what's going on here.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, we're cleaning up the bodies without removing them so we would see relationships of how they were placed in the grave, and this is a process of cleaning up so you reveal all the information in the grave, how the bodies are placed, what elements are related to each other. These are very detailed work and hard tools are only used in the loosening up of the dirt in between the bodies. But then it's very detailed work on removing the material so you don't remove cultural elements in association. You try to recover exactly that, the associations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood. And can you tell if you're in this picture?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, I am in the picture, at the left of it. And next to me is assisting is one of the French security guards. The rest of the people are -- they are on top, looking down. You can only see her hair basically. It's an anthropologist from Florida. It's an oriental last name. I don't recall her last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then at the bottom of the picture is an archaeologist, last name Moscosko and the lady that is -- with her back to the camera is Horena. I don't recall her last name, but she is an archaeologist, a forensic anthropologist, from the USA. I think she's from one of the -- a state in the centre of the US.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Do you need any more details?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just if you could be clear about which one you is. You said the left side of the picture.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: The left side of the picture. It's the only face you can see here, with a beard, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think I see the only person with a beard. Thank you. Now, in Dr. Haglund's report on this particular grave which, in our case, is P1833, he notes that the minimum number of individuals found in that grave was 132. And is that roughly what you reflect about the number of -- minimum number of individuals that was in this grave?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that number was -- well, I -- I concur. This is a number -- with estimation, field estimation, of the minimum amount of bodies. In this particular site, the recovery was precise and well done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you also worked in the morgue or what I believe you called the laboratory that examined these bodies along with the forensic pathologists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from both your work in this excavation and in the lab, do you remember finding cloth ligatures around the wrists of any of these victims from this grave?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly from this grave but I do remember seeing the cloth on the -- on the section that you will call the eyes of the body as -- what we would call a blindfold. Also, I do remember seeing wrist, wire wrist, improvised handcuff, with a sort of wire that you would use to hang your clothing for drying, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to try to be clear, the wire handcuffs, could that have been at the Cerska grave where people were just shot over the edge of a road and dirt poured on top of them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: When you say "Cerska," are you talking about the side road that was extended?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just the location and the name that you call the grave, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in Dr. Haglund's report, going back to the Pilica, the grave we have in front of us, he notes that ligatures were recovered from 82 individuals, and the wrists of 77 were bound and that ligatures were associated with some additional remains. Now, would those cloth ligature have been -- or were they saved as part of the evidence in your work?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This grave is well dug. As you can see, it's a lot of detailed work on it. So the relationship of elements is going to be much -- is going to be precise. Perhaps there is a lot of photographs showing exactly what you're asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And do you --

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you also recall in the lab or the morgue the doctors and/or the anthropologists takes samples of the bones for potential DNA testing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: We cut a segment of the tibia about 1 centimetre by 1 and a half centimetres of most of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: It was a protocol we tried to follow, to cut at the same site, the same height of the shaft of the bone. But sometimes we have isolated bones and so forth, so I don't believe that the protocol applied to all the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the investigation has revealed in this case that from five graves associated with this Pilica grave, associated by DNA connections between the five graves and this Pilica grave, as well as matching of cloth from ligatures in some of the five graves matching with the Pilica grave, the evidence here is that 1.611 people were identified through DNA in those five secondary graves, I'll call them, and that each of those five graves was associated, either through a DNA match or a cloth match, to your Pilica grave. If good DNA matches or good DNA was taken from the secondary graves and cloth was found in those secondary graves, from your experience, could that be tested up against the DNA found in the primary grave that you did, where you took DNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that the witness has been qualified on an expert on DNA. He has previously testified as to his inability to be an expert as to textiles. So cloth, I believe, is sa textile, so I think we're asking the witness to go beyond areas that he might be able to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. One second, Please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think a doctor that sends a test out, some microscopic test, needs to be an expert in that test to know if can he use the result of that test in his work, and that's simply the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just re-read the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The question doesn't require DNA expertise. The question started with, "if DNA was taken, what then could be done," and that is within the knowledge of this witness's experience. Therefore, you may answer the question. Perhaps, Mr. McCloskey, it was a very long introduction. Perhaps if you repeat but then the question only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Del Pino, if good DNA was obtained from your work at the Pilica grave and good DNA was obtained in the five associated graves that I'm talking about, could that DNA be compared and potentially match and make a connection between the secondary grave and the primary grave?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I need to -- yes. The answer is yes. And I need to remark that the DNA technology is -- we tried to implement it in Chile in 1989 in cases of missing people. So I'm very familiar with the reasoning behind the DNA, even though I'm not a biochemist. But, yes, it can be related.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does it surprise you that now, some 18 or 19 years after you were taking DNA samples, that 1.751 people from these graves I've described to you have been identified through DNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: I am not surprised. DNA is a modern technology to help to match genetic characteristics. I'm not surprised. This is good information. Glad to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you ever hear after your work there that a Serbian soldier named Drazen Erdemovic estimated that 1.200 Muslims were killed near this grave and that another 500 were to be killed in the town of Pilica for a total of about 1.700 people? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID DEL PINO
utterances.text: No. I was trying to be a very cut-and-dry scientist. I didn't want to involve myself with that information. I wanted to discover it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there's no need to go through all the evidence and ask this witness whether he's aware of all that. That's not something which is related to his testimony. And, of course, although you may elicit evidence from a witness which supports your case, it's not supposed not to be either repetitive evidence or -- there should be at least some kind of a link. You are moving too far away and that's the opinion of this Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions? But often I would have questions and perhaps it's better for me to put them first --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Del Pino, you explained us that Mr. Haglund was absent with some frequency. Did it ever happen that you needed his guidance as the team leader where, due to his unavailability, you had any problems in performing your task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of how that happened and how you resolved that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, the end result stalled the dig because there was no direction. We stopped digging the grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was your problem, what you couldn't resolve without his presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't exactly recall. Perhaps it might have been the need for equipment, covering the grave, rain protection. I don't exactly recall but I recall being stalled because there was no -- nobody to speak about. We have no -- our boss wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And once he returned, did you then continue where you had stopped or what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We normally continue with -- we stopped and -- yeah, that was what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the elements you told us about, the absence of Mr. Haglund -- no. Let me strike that. Could you tell us, the discarded clothing, did that have any effect on the results, such as that you considered them to be wrong conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No wrong conclusion. I don't think so. But incomplete conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You think it could have been better but what you found is not wrong. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the same for the time Mr. Haglund spent in his media attention. Did this have any consequences as far as the outcome of your work is concerned?

I really don't know the depth of the consequences, but sometimes you have to speed up the work because media or slow down the work. I don't know. It's not good for archaeology to be following the pace of external elements. An archaeological dig needs to follow its own dynamics, not waiting for -- accelerating the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think that in accelerating the work for those reasons that inappropriate risks were taken to reach wrong conclusions?

utterances.text: In archaeology I don't think wrong conclusions but incomplete conclusions. You lose evidence. When you touch -- when you touch your grave-site, you are at the moment of collection of evidence, collection of elements. If you don't collect the most you can, you collect incomplete evidence, hardly wrong evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But even if you have incomplete evidence, that could result in wrong conclusions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are you aware of any -- could you give us an instance of where the lack of completeness led you to conclusions which you consider not to be sound?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've told us about the quantity of clothing that was discarded in this way. Could you also tell us -- I think you told us that you attended or participated in exhumations in 15 to 20 sites. In how many of these 15 or 20 sites did this discarding of clothing happened?
